title: The Monty Hall Problem and the Limits of Probabilistic Intuition
question: Why do nearly all of us, including experts, get the Monty Hall problem wrong?
summary: Switching doors wins two thirds of the time, yet intuition insists on 50-50. The puzzle shows that evidence depends on the process that produced it.
content:
The Setup

You face three doors: one hides a car, two hide goats. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is, opens a different door to reveal a goat and offers you the chance to switch. Should you? Almost everyone says it makes no difference, a 50-50 choice. In fact switching wins two thirds of the time.

Why Switching Works

Your first pick is right with probability 1/3, and that does not change when the host acts. The remaining 2/3 of probability was spread across the other two doors; the host, constrained never to open the car, concentrates all of it onto the one door left. Imagine 100 doors: you pick one, the host opens 98 goats. Few would still believe the last unopened door is no better than yours.

The Hidden Assumption

The answer depends on the host's behaviour. Because the host must open a goat door, his action carries information. If he opened a door at random and happened to reveal a goat, switching would be a true 50-50. The same observation means different things depending on the process that generated it, which is the heart of Bayesian reasoning.

The Public Reaction

When Marilyn vos Savant published the correct answer in 1990, thousands of readers, including many PhDs, wrote in to insist she was wrong. Even Paul Erdős reportedly refused to accept it until shown a simulation. The error is persistent because it feels like a clear application of symmetry: two doors, so equal odds.

Lessons

We tend to treat evidence as a snapshot of the world rather than the output of a process. Medical test results, courtroom statistics, and news selection effects all fall into the same trap. Reframing in terms of frequencies, such as 100 doors or 1000 simulated games, makes the right answer intuitive.

perspectives.title: Bayesian Statistics
perspectives.description: The host's opening is evidence whose strength depends on his strategy. Updating correctly requires modelling how the data were generated, not merely what was seen.

perspectives.title: Cognitive Psychology
perspectives.description: People anchor on the surface symmetry of two remaining options. Natural-frequency formats dramatically improve performance, suggesting our minds handle counts better than single-case probabilities.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Probability
perspectives.description: The puzzle exposes the gap between frequentist and subjective readings: is 2/3 a long-run frequency or a rational degree of belief?

perspectives.title: Education
perspectives.description: Experiential simulation beats verbal argument. Learners who play the game repeatedly converge on switching, even when explanations failed.
